title: Very, very humble (Avot 4:4)
hookLine: Levitas of Yavneh: be very, very humble
tomorrow: learning that stays in your notes: what's it for?

cards: At a curtain call the whole cast does the same thing at once: they bend. Applause pours down, and the body answers by getting lower.
Rabbi Levitas of Yavneh has a short saying in Avot, and he doubles a word in it: me'od me'od hevei shefal ruach. Very, very, be humble of spirit.

teach.b: Why twice? Hebrew can say very once. Levitas says it twice, and teachers often answer with Maimonides.
For most traits, Maimonides says, aim for the middle: not stingy, not lavish.

teach.h: PRIDE: GO TO THE FAR END.
teach.b: But with pride, and with anger, he says go all the way to the far end; with arrogance, the middle isn't safe. So me'od me'od isn't modest-ish. It's very, very.
Levitas gives a blunt reason: the hope of a mortal is the worm. That sounds grim, but it's a leveling line.
Every body ends in the same earth, the well-known and the forgotten, which makes looking down on anyone a little absurd. And shefal ruach doesn't mean thinking you're worthless.
Shefal is low; ruach is spirit. A spirit close to the ground: steady, not puffed up, so a compliment can land and leave you standing.
Like a bow at the curtain call. You take the applause, and you get lower. Notice that the bow comes after the applause, not instead of it.

how: Jewish ethical writing, from Maimonides to the Mussar teachers, treats humility as a trait to practice daily; Avot 4:4 is often quoted as its sharpest form.

o: a little, in a moderate and balanced amount
to the extreme: humility taken all the way
loud praise shouted at the end of a show

p: with pride, go to the far end

s: shefal ruach is a spirit kept low and steady, not a verdict on your worth.
Maimonides says that with pride, aim for the far end, not the middle
with arrogance, the middle isn't safe.
Levitas says the word only once
me'od me'od: he says it twice.

games.q: you get promoted over a coworker who's been there longer. the next morning, what fits Levitas?
o: thank her, ask her advice, and keep your spirit low.
keep saying you don't deserve it, again and again.
avoid the subject so nobody has any feelings about it.
games.why: shefal ruach is a low spirit, not a low opinion of yourself: steady enough to take the promotion and still look up to others.

practice: Sit tall, then let your chin dip slightly, as if bowing to someone you respect. Feel the back of your neck lengthen and your shoulders soften.
Stay there, low and steady, and let each breath settle you a little closer to the ground.

wordCard.voice: Very. Levitas's me'od, said twice: humility taken all the way, not halfway.

orig.note: Hebrew: very, very; Levitas of Yavneh doubles it for humility.

carryVoice: Carry this: very, very humble, like a bow at the end, lower and still standing. Rest well.
